title: Scientific or Technological Advancement - SR&ED Glossary
description: Learn what qualifies as a Scientific or Technological Advancement in our Canadian SR&ED glossary to strengthen your R&D tax credit claim.
summary: Scientific or technological advancement is a core test for Canada's SR&ED tax incentives under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Canadian businesses claiming federal or provincial R&D credits must show their work generated new scientific or technological knowledge; even failed experiments can qualify when contemporaneous records show why an approach could not succeed.

body.text: Scientific or technological advancement is a core test for Canada's SR&ED tax incentives under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Canadian businesses claiming federal or provincial R&D credits must show their work generated new scientific or technological knowledge; even failed experiments can qualify when contemporaneous records show why an approach could not succeed.
Executive Statutory and Legislative Framework

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture is anchored by the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which represents the single largest federal source of industrial innovation funding in the country, supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada under the statutory authority of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), the SR&ED program operates not as a discretionary grant application, but as a statutory entitlement integrated directly into the taxpayer's annual income tax return.

The legislative foundation of the federal SR&ED regime rests on three interconnected provisions of the Income Tax Act and its accompanying Income Tax Regulations. First, Subsection 248(1) codifies the statutory definition of SR&ED, establishing the substantive scientific and technological criteria governing what constitutes qualifying basic research, applied research, experimental development, and eligible support work. Second, Section 37 governs the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, representing the first statutory incentive by permitting taxpayers to pool current expenditures under Paragraph 37(1)(a) and eligible capital expenditures under Paragraph 37(1)(b) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Balances within the Subsection 37(1) expenditure pool may be deducted in full to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Within this same statutory division, Subsection 37(11) establishes the strict statutory filing deadline, requiring prescribed forms to be filed within 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date, while Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) governs the eligibility of materials transformed when a claimant elects to use the proxy method.

Third, Section 127 governs the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) mechanics, which provide the second statutory incentive by granting taxpayers an ITC calculated as a specified percentage of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of each taxation year. Subsection 127(9) codifies the core definitions of "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool," "contract payment," and "specified percentage". Related statutory mechanisms include Subsection 127(8) governing the allocation of partnership ITCs, Subsection 127(13) governing agreements to transfer qualified expenditures between non-arm's length parties (as defined under Section 251), and Subsection 127(26) governing the exclusion of unpaid amounts. Where R&D is conducted through a partnership structure, Subsection 96(1) and Paragraph 96(1)(e.1) dictate how SR&ED expenditure deductions must be claimed at the partnership level rather than flowing into the individual partners' separate Section 37 pools.
Enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1)

On March 26, 2026, Parliament enacted the most sweeping structural expansion of the federal SR&ED regime in over a decade when Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent. Tabled by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue to implement key innovation and tax measures originating in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the 2024 federal budget, and Budget 2025 (Canada Strong), Bill C-15 fundamentally recalibrated the expenditure limits, corporate eligibility rules, capital property treatment, and administrative review procedures of the SR&ED program.

Except where specifically noted for administrative processes, the primary legislative amendments enacted under Bill C-15 apply retroactively and prospectively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (meaning taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024; for a calendar-year corporation, this encompasses the taxation year beginning January 1, 2025, and all subsequent taxation years). For taxation years that commenced prior to December 16, 2024, the pre-Bill C-15 statutory rules continue to govern the calculation of eligible expenditures and investment tax credits.

The legislative overhaul enacted through Bill C-15 introduces six structural transformations to the Canadian innovation landscape. First, Parliament doubled the maximum annual qualified SR&ED expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% federal ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for qualifying corporations and their associated corporate groups. As a direct mathematical consequence, the maximum annual refundable federal cash benefit available to a qualifying corporation has doubled from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range over which the enhanced expenditure limit is reduced has been expanded from the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to $15,000,000–$75,000,000. Third, Bill C-15 permits CCPCs and their associated corporate groups to elect to have their enhanced expenditure limit phase-out calculated using a three-year average gross revenue test rather than prior-year taxable capital.

Fourth, breaking with the historical statutory restriction that confined the 35% refundable credit exclusively to private CCPCs, Bill C-15 extends access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC (up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test. Fifth, reversing the 2014 legislative repeal of capital costs, Bill C-15 restores eligibility for qualifying expenditures on depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024, as well as qualifying equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation. Sixth, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA operationalised a formal, optional pre-claim approval regime using Form T1322, enabling eligible businesses to obtain upfront eligibility determinations on up to three proposed projects within eight weeks prior to commencing R&D work.

Alongside these SR&ED-specific reforms, Bill C-15 enacted complementary capital cost allowance (CCA) incentives that interact directly with corporate R&D infrastructure planning. Specifically, Bill C-15 provides 100% immediate expensing for qualifying acquisitions of property in Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software) if acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027. Furthermore, Bill C-15 temporarily reinstated the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII), providing an enhanced first-year CCA deduction for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030, with a progressive phase-out scheduled starting in 2030 and full elimination after 2033 (whereas under prior rules, the AII was being phased out between 2024 and 2027).

body.text: Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryover Mechanics

Calculating a federal SR&ED claim requires executing two mathematically distinct yet interrelated statutory computations: first, determining the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Section 37; and second, determining the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" eligible to earn Investment Tax Credits under Section 127. While the Section 37 deduction pool carries forward indefinitely from year to year until deducted by the taxpayer, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool under Subsection 127(9) is an annual calculation that terminates at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over as an expenditure pool to subsequent years. Instead, the dollar amount of unused Investment Tax Credits generated by that annual pool may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Part I federal tax payable.
The Enhanced 35% ITC Regime: Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs

Under Subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) and the amendments enacted by Bill C-15, qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an enhanced federal ITC of 35% (the 15% specified percentage plus a 20% addition under Subsection 127(10.1)) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000. Where a corporation is associated with one or more other corporations in a taxation year, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared and allocated across the associated corporate group.

For qualifying corporations operating within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the enhanced 35% ITC earned on current expenditures (and on the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount) is 100% refundable in cash to the extent that the credit exceeds the corporation's federal Part I tax liability for the year. Qualified expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its available annual expenditure limit earn the basic federal ITC rate of 15%.
Phase-Out Mechanics: Prior-Year Taxable Capital vs. Three-Year Average Gross Revenue

Historically, for taxation years beginning prior to December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit was phased out where the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (and its associated group) exceeded $10,000,000, reaching complete elimination at $50,000,000. In the statutory mechanics of the Income Tax Act, that legacy phase-out mirrored the qualifying income limit reduction formula:

where A equalled nil if prior-year taxable capital was less than or equal to $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeded $10,000,000. Where a CCPC's qualifying income limit was reduced to zero because its prior-year taxable capital reached or exceeded $50,000,000, the CCPC ceased to be a qualifying corporation and lost entitlement to refundable ITCs.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 expanded the taxable capital phase-out corridor to begin at $15,000,000 and terminate at $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada across the associated group. Over this $60,000,000 span ($75,000,000 minus $15,000,000), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases linearly by $1 for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is less than or equal to $15,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000

Crucially, the interplay between balance-sheet capitalisation and R&D eligibility previously penalised capital-intensive scale-ups—such as biotechnology, semiconductor, clean technology, and deep-tech hardware ventures—that raised substantial preferred equity or convertible debt. Under Part I.3 taxable capital definitions, retained earnings, share capital, and debt obligations inflate a corporation's taxable capital employed in Canada even when the enterprise is pre-revenue or operating at a substantial loss. Under the pre-2025 regime, a venture-backed CCPC that closed a $55,000,000 financing round was immediately stripped of its 35% refundable status and relegated to the 15% non-refundable credit in the following taxation year.

Bill C-15 resolves this structural distortion through two complementary mechanisms. First, raising the upper taxable capital threshold to $75,000,000 preserves enhanced eligibility for growing mid-market CCPCs that were previously pushed out of the enhanced rate. Second, permitting CCPCs and their associated groups to elect to calculate their expenditure limit phase-out based on a three-year average gross revenue test (identical to the test introduced for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations) decouples balance-sheet equity raises from SR&ED refundability. Consequently, a growing CCPC that has accumulated significant taxable capital exceeding $75,000,000 through equity financing while maintaining a modest commercial revenue profile can elect the revenue-based phase-out test and retain access to its $6,000,000 expenditure limit at the 35% refundable rate. Because the revenue election is not automatically superior for every corporate profile—such as a high-revenue, asset-light software CCPC whose taxable capital remains below $15,000,000—accountants and SR&ED advisors must compare both limit calculations using the actual corporate structure, revenue history, associated companies, and eligible expenditures.

Similarly, extending the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) eliminates the historical tax penalty associated with listing on a Canadian stock exchange, where domestic public technology, biotechnology, and clean-energy issuers previously lost their refundable SR&ED status solely by virtue of being public corporations. For ECPCs, eligibility for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is determined using the three-year average gross revenue test, with the refundable expenditure limit gradually phased out as average gross revenue increases.
The Basic 15% ITC Regime and Non-Corporate Claimants

All claimants that do not qualify for the enhanced 35% credit earn the basic federal ITC at a specified percentage of 15% (a rate established for taxation years after 2013, following the pro-rated reduction for taxation years straddling January 1, 2014). Claimants subject to the basic 15% ITC rate encompass corporations other than qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries of multinational enterprises and large domestic public or private corporations exceeding the $75,000,000 taxable capital or gross revenue phase-out thresholds), qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their available annual expenditure limit, sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts.

For corporations subject to the basic 15% rate, the resulting ITC is non-refundable and may only be applied to reduce federal Part I income tax payable in the current year, carried back 3 years, or carried forward 20 years. Individuals and trusts earning the 15% ITC claim their credit using Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) rather than corporate Schedule 31; individuals (other than trusts), and trusts whose beneficiaries are all such individuals or qualifying corporations, may qualify for partial (40%) refundability on unused credits earned on current expenditures under the individual refundability rules of the Income Tax Act.
Partnership Rules and Structural Limitations

Where SR&ED is carried out by a partnership, special statutory constraints apply under Subsection 96(1), Paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and Subsection 127(8) of the Income Tax Act. Because a partnership is a flow-through calculation entity rather than a distinct taxable person, the partnership itself must file a single Form T661 reporting all of its SR&ED expenditures for the fiscal period rather than an individual partner's share.

The pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Subsection 37(1) must be deducted at the partnership level in computing the partnership's net income or loss for the fiscal period under Paragraph 96(1)(e.1); individual partners are strictly prohibited from adding partnership SR&ED costs to their own separate Section 37 pools. Furthermore, while the ITC calculated on the partnership's qualified expenditures is allocated to the individual partners at the end of the partnership's fiscal period pursuant to Subsection 127(8), partnership credits earn the basic 15% rate and are typically non-refundable. Consequently, for businesses conducting significant R&D activity, incorporating as a CCPC before commencing R&D and claiming SR&ED produces a markedly superior cash-flow and tax outcome compared to operating as an unincorporated partnership.

body.text: Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria and Jurisprudence

To qualify for federal and provincial SR&ED tax incentives, claimed activities must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. An "SR&ED project" comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements, pursued through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals.

The CRA recognises four statutory categories of qualifying work under Subsection 248(1). The first category is basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in mind; because most basic research occurs at universities and research institutes, it represents the least common category for corporate claims. The second category is applied research, which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and largest commercial category is experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new, or improve existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The fourth category is eligible support work—covering engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development. The CRA determines the eligibility of any project at the level necessary to properly recognise all the work required for the attempted scientific or technological advancement, including eligible support work, while strictly excluding routine coding, standard software implementation, routine debugging, normal product development, market research, quality control, and commercial production.
Judicial Foundation: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen

The authoritative judicial interpretation of Subsection 248(1) was established by Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, [1998] T.C.J. No. 340. Following the earlier legislative evolution of the program signaled in the May 23, 1985 Budget Papers (Securing Economic Renewal, tabled by Finance Minister Michael H. Wilson) and Government of Canada News Release 92-088 (December 2, 1992), Judge Bowman articulated a five-step sequential test at paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic—universally known in Canadian tax law and CRA administrative practice as the "Five Questions"—to determine whether a project constitutes eligible SR&ED.

Under the first question of Northwest Hydraulic, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or techniques accessible to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Under the second question, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Under the third question, the inquiry evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the systematic formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiments or analyses. Under the fourth question, the court asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, meaning the generation of new scientific or technological knowledge that advances understanding—importantly, even when a trial fails and a hypothesis is rejected, preserving the data of failure establishes knowledge gained regarding why a technical approach cannot succeed under given constraints. Finally, under the fifth question, the court evaluates whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed.

In its current administrative guidance (Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives), the CRA presents simplified information organized around Two Requirements—referred to as the "Why" and the "How"—to determine if there is SR&ED. The CRA explicitly confirms in its historical policy guidance and its Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) that both the two requirements ("Why" and "How") and the five questions are derived directly from the statutory definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which did not change, providing a common language for claimants and CRA officials. The "Why" requirement synthesizes the technological uncertainty and technological advancement criteria, while the "How" requirement synthesizes the systematic investigation, hypothesis testing, and contemporaneous documentation criteria.
Key Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence on Software, Engineering, and Evidence

Subsequent jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada has rigorously policed the boundary between eligible experimental development and ineligible routine engineering, particularly within software engineering, systems integration, and industrial manufacturing. In Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed the taxpayer's SR&ED appeal concerning software development activities. The Court scrutinized the claimant's technical narratives and witness testimony, ruling that inflated descriptions of commercial software features constituted a mere "statement of business fact" rather than evidence of underlying technological uncertainty. Crucially, the taxpayer's own documentation and testimony described its development work using phrases such as "trial and error," "standard web page programming," and "a commonly used tool". Together with the Tax Court of Canada's earlier decision in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, Hypercube demonstrates that when taxpayers use such language, their own words prove routine engineering and sink the appeal.

The legal dividing line established by Hypercube and Zeuter between unsystematic "trial and error" (which is fatal to an SR&ED claim) and "systematic investigation" (which qualifies) is whether each failed technical option is followed by a rigorous analysis of why it failed before the next hypothesis is formulated and tested. For example, in software engineering, claiming high-level application development fails, whereas framing the uncertainty as an architectural incompatibility—not readily resolvable with existing, accessible products—that required systematic research and experimentation to devise code allowing data sharing between .NET and Java environments satisfies the statutory threshold.

Similarly, in Concept Danat Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 32, and 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015, Docket 2012-3634), the Tax Court of Canada reaffirmed Chief Justice Bowman's foundational principles in Northwest Hydraulic (paragraph 16). The Courts consistently police the failure mode of documents created retroactively for an audit, placing decisive evidentiary weight on contemporaneous technical artifacts generated during the R&D—such as source-code repository logs, cryptographic commit hashes, immutable timestamps, hypotheses logs, and failed test data. Whether in industrial manufacturing and cured-in-place pipe rehabilitation engineering (as illustrated by the practical case of Formadrain Inc.), biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, or backend software architecture, machine learning model development, and real-time systems, the tax benefit strictly follows the qualifying experimental work rather than creating it.
Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Calculation Methodologies, and Capital Restoration

Once a project's scientific or technological eligibility is established under Subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable SR&ED expenditures for the Subsection 37(1) deduction pool (Part 3 of Form T661) and its qualified SR&ED expenditures for the Subsection 127(9) Investment Tax Credit pool (Part 4 of Form T661).
Election of Overhead Calculation Methodology: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, the claimant must choose (elect) to calculate its SR&ED expenditures using either the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). This election must be made for each taxation year when Form T661 is first filed for the year, and whether the claimant elects the proxy method or the traditional method, the choice is irrevocable for the taxation year. If the claimant is a member of a partnership that elects to use the proxy method to calculate income from the partnership, the election is valid only if made on behalf of all members of the partnership by an authorized partner who had the authority to act for the partnership.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not need to specifically identify, track, or allocate overhead and other indirect expenditures for SR&ED. In lieu of itemised overhead, the claimant includes a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—calculated under the Income Tax Regulations in Part 5 of Form T661. Since 2014 (having been reduced from the 65% rate applicable in earlier tax years such as 2007), the prescribed proxy percentage has been 55% (reported on Line 820 in Part 5, Section B) of the eligible SR&ED salary base calculated using directly engaged SR&ED salaries and wages, subject to statutory specified-employee salary-base restrictions and the overall proxy cap.

A fundamental statutory distinction governs the accounting and tax treatment of the PPA. Because the PPA is a notional amount used solely to calculate qualified expenditures for the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit (transferred from Part 5 to Line 502 in Part 4 of Form T661), the PPA is not added to the Subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Instead, the actual underlying overhead expenses represented by the PPA—such as office supplies, general-purpose office equipment, heat, water, electricity, telephones, salaries or wages for support staff not directly engaged in SR&ED, employer's share of related benefits, travel and training, property taxes, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment, and contract costs for non-SR&ED support work—are deducted as ordinary business expenses in computing regular business income and cannot be included in the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant does not calculate a salary base or PPA in Part 5 and does not need to calculate the overall proxy cap. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, and allocate all overhead and other expenditures (claimed on Line 360 of Part 3, Section B, and allocated by project on Line 758 of Part 6) that are directly related and incremental to the performing of SR&ED—meaning eligible expenditures that the business would not have incurred if the SR&ED had not been carried out. Under the Traditional Method, eligible overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 include incremental facility heat, water, electricity, maintenance, employer's share of related benefits, travel and training, contract costs for work that is not itself SR&ED (for example, contract costs for the work of electricians, welders, or mechanics that are directly related and incremental to performing SR&ED), and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time. Overhead claimed under the Traditional Method is both included in the Subsection 37(1)(a) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and eligible for the Section 127 ITC. While most software and technology companies use the Proxy Method because it is simpler and yields a high 55% notional overhead credit, enterprises whose actual incremental overhead exceeds the 55% PPA ceiling should model both methods before filing their first claim for the year.

body.text: Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED performed in Canada (along with a portion of supporting staff time directly engaged in eligible support work) are claimed in Part 3, Section B on Line 300, while unpaid salaries or wages that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are reported on Line 315.

Special statutory restrictions apply to specified employees (shareholder-employees owning 10% or more of the shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or individuals not dealing at arm's length with the corporation). When calculating the Part 5 Salary Base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount, a specified employee's includable salary is restricted to the lesser of 75% of their total salary or wages and 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), prorated for the number of days employed in the taxation year. For a 2026 taxation year-end, where the YMPE is $74,600, that statutory ceiling is $186,500:

To illustrate this restriction with an exact numerical example: if an owner-manager (specified employee) earns a salary of $300,000 in 2026 and is directly engaged in SR&ED, 75% of $300,000 equals $225,000, which is capped at $186,500 in Part 5. When combined with $400,000 of directly engaged SR&ED salaries paid to arm's length employees, the total Part 5 salary base equals $586,500.
Materials, Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Non-Arm's Length Transfers

Claimants may deduct and claim ITCs on the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed (allowed under the proxy method effective after February 23, 1998, pursuant to Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Income Tax Act) in performing SR&ED. However, where materials transformed or SR&ED property are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules trigger an income inclusion on Line 231 of T2 Schedule 1.

For contract expenditures where an arm's length contractor performs SR&ED on behalf of the claimant in Canada, and for third-party payments (each requiring a separate Schedule A attached to Form T661), 100% of the eligible contract or third-party expenditure is deductible in the Subsection 37(1)(a) pool in Part 3, whereas only 80% of the expenditure is included in the Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool in Part 4 to earn the Investment Tax Credit (Part 4 strips 20% for the credit). Where a claimant enters into SR&ED contracts with performers not dealing at arm's length (as defined in Section 251), those expenditures are entered on Line 345 of Section B in Part 3; they are deductible in the Section 37 pool, but earn no Investment Tax Credit unless the parties execute an agreement to transfer qualified expenditures under Subsection 127(13). Under the CRA's revised Total Qualified Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (Appendix A.2, Example 1, and Appendix D.1), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is included in the performer's total qualified SR&ED expenditures for determining the transferable amount under Subsection 127(13).
Restored Capital Expenditures and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15, Parliament restored SR&ED eligibility for depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024, and qualifying equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Expenditures for depreciable property or for the right to use property acquired before December 16, 2024, do not qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, and claimants may only include lease costs of equipment for capital expenditures that the performer made after December 15, 2024. This restoration is particularly impactful for hardware-intensive R&D projects, including artificial intelligence and machine learning companies acquiring Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and compute infrastructure, laboratory apparatus in biotechnology, and cleantech or manufacturing prototyping equipment.

The statutory mechanics of the restored capital and lease regime depend on the percentage of operating time the asset is used in SR&ED. Equipment used all or substantially all (ASA)—defined as 90% or more of its operating time—for SR&ED qualifies for full capital expenditure treatment under Paragraph 37(1)(b) and Subsection 127(9) (reported on restored Lines 390 and 400 in Part 3, Section B, and in the restored Capital Expenditures column of Part 4, including Lines 496 and 504). Similarly, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used 90% or more for SR&ED are claimed in full on restored Line 350 of Part 3.

Where equipment is used partially for SR&ED and partially for commercial operations, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, can produce a partial ITC in Part 4 where statutory conditions are met. For leased equipment used 50% to under 90% for SR&ED after December 15, 2024, claimants electing the Proxy Method claim half (50%) of the lease costs on Line 355, whereas claimants electing the Traditional Method enter 0 on Line 355 and instead claim the eligible SR&ED lease costs for equipment used less than 90% of the time on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures. Land and buildings (including Class 1 manufacturing and processing buildings) remain strictly excluded from the restored SR&ED capital expenditure rules, and used equipment is treated differently for Section 37 deduction and Section 127 ITC purposes. Because of the technical precision of these rules, businesses must contemporaneously document the accounting treatment, the exact available-for-use date, the percentage of SR&ED operating time, and any subsequent sale or conversion to commercial use.
Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 127(26)) and Government Assistance Grinding

Under Subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act, unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages already excluded on Line 315) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in the year and must be removed from qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 520 of Part 4 (and reported in Section 2 of Schedule B). This ensures that the unpaid expenditure does not earn an ITC until the taxation year in which it is actually paid; furthermore, when an unpaid arm's length contract or third-party payment is paid in a subsequent year, only 80% of the amount paid is added to qualified SR&ED expenditures in that subsequent year.

Additionally, under Subsection 127(9), an amount that would otherwise be a qualified expenditure must be reduced by any government assistance (including provincial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of the SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Conversely, if the claimant repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its deductible SR&ED expenditure pool, the repayments are added back in Section 1 of Schedule B and reported on Lines 445, 452, and 454 in Part 3 of Form T661.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal-Provincial Stacking

Across Canada, provincial and territorial governments administer complementary R&D tax incentives that interact directly with the federal SR&ED regime. Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial credits claimed on SR&ED expenditures reduce ("grind") the qualified expenditure pool eligible for the federal 35% or 15% ITC. Furthermore, any provincial tax credit earned on the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in the current or prior year must be added back to taxable income on Lines 290–294 of T2 Schedule 1.
Quebec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Revolution and CDAEIA Transition

In the Quebec Budget 2025–2026 (For a Strong Québec, published on March 25, 2025), the Quebec government enacted a landmark restructuring of provincial innovation funding. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec consolidated and replaced eight separate legacy R&D tax credit programs—including the Tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (which previously offered rates between 14% and 30%, decreasing linearly above a $3,000,000 asset/cap threshold), the Tax credit for university research or research carried out by public research centres, the Tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, and the Tax credit for fees and dues paid to research consortiums—into a single unified incentive: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).

Unlike the previous Quebec system where rates varied from 14% to 30% based on company size and asset characteristics, CRIC offers a universal, 100% refundable two-tier rate structure to startups, SMBs, and multinational corporations alike. Under Tier 1, claimants earn a 30% refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold. Under Tier 2, claimants earn a 20% refundable tax credit on all eligible expenditures in excess of that $1,000,000 tier.

Beyond rate unification, CRIC introduces three structural expansions. First, CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities not eligible under federal SR&ED—bridging the commercialization "Valley of Death" by funding product design, regulatory testing, and market validation, while integrating with Quebec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) (with statutory rules ensuring that the Quebec nexus ratio is not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold). Second, CRIC restores eligibility for capital expenditures on R&D laboratory equipment, software development infrastructure, specialised manufacturing equipment for prototyping, and testing/validation equipment in Quebec. Third, CRIC replaces the legacy asset-based exclusion threshold with a reformed per-employee formula: the CRIC exclusion threshold is now the greater of $50,000 or the Quebec basic personal amount per eligible employee, prorated based on each employee's time spent on R&D and pre-commercialization activities.
For example, in a 2025 calculation where the basic personal amount is $18,571, a company employing 10 full-time R&D employees has an exclusion threshold of:

meaning only expenditures above $185,710 qualify for the credit. On $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the threshold, a Quebec AI or technology company can generate $500,000 in provincial CRIC (30% × $1,000,000 + 20% × $1,000,000) alongside $700,000 in federal SR&ED (before assistance grinding), yielding over $1,200,000 in combined support when stacked with CDAEIA.

In parallel, Quebec rebalanced its Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE), co-administered by Investissement Québec (Invest Québec). CDAE is restricted to Quebec-based IT and digital companies that derive at least 75% of their revenue from IT activities and 50% from software or digital product development, maintain at least six eligible full-time technical employees (startups under two years old qualify once they reach the six-employee threshold during the claim year), and hold an annual certificate from Investissement Québec. Under 2024 rules, CDAE provided a 30% credit (24% refundable + 6% non-refundable) on technical salaries up to $83,333 per employee. Starting in 2025 and transitioning into the Credit for the Development of E-Business – Innovation and Automation (CDAEIA) in 2026, Quebec eliminated the salary cap, introduced a per-employee exclusion threshold, shifted the 30% rate to 20% refundable and 10% non-refundable, and refocused eligibility onto AI-driven automation, data and analytics innovation, and cloud infrastructure development. While expenditures eligible for a Quebec R&D tax credit are excluded from double-counting under CDAE/CDAEIA, Quebec software companies frequently claim experimental R&D under SR&ED/CRIC and commercial digital/AI development under CDAE/CDAEIA in the same fiscal year.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and Dual-Pool Stacking

In Ontario, corporations combine federal SR&ED credits with provincial credits administered by the CRA and claimed via provincial schedules filed electronically with the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 566, provides an 8% refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016, with a prorated rate for taxation years straddling June 1, 2016) for small to medium-sized CCPCs on qualifying SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure cap of $3,000,000. To qualify for the OITC, the corporation must be a CCPC with a permanent establishment in Ontario that files federal Form T661 and is eligible for the federal Section 127 ITC; the $3,000,000 OITC cap is phased out for corporations (and associated groups) with prior-year taxable capital between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario. Available to all corporations regardless of size or CCPC status, the ORDTC reduces Ontario corporate income tax payable and can be carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years. Third, corporations partnering with an approved Ontario research institute can claim the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), which provides a 20% refundable tax credit on eligible R&D contract expenditures. (Separately, for general corporate income tax context, Ontario's Small Business Deduction provides a 3.2% reduced corporate tax rate on the first $500,000 of active business income compared to the 11.5% general rate, phasing out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of taxable capital, alongside interactive digital media tax credits of 35%–40%.)
When stacking Ontario and federal R&D credits, the government assistance grinding rules produce two standard effective recovery rates on total SR&ED expenditures (including proxy overhead):

Thus, a non-CCPC in Ontario receives 17.98% of total SR&ED expenditures including proxy overhead, while a qualifying CCPC earning the enhanced 35% federal rate receives 42.29% of total SR&ED expenditures including proxy overhead.
Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Operating since January 1, 2021, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (AB IEG) is a refundable provincial R&D incentive integrated into the Alberta corporate tax system and claimed when filing the annual corporate tax return. Linked directly to expenditures verified as eligible for the federal SR&ED program by the CRA, the AB IEG supports up to $4,000,000 in annual qualifying R&D spending in Alberta through a two-tier incremental structure.

Claimants receive an 8% base payment on qualifying Alberta R&D expenditures up to their "base spending level"—defined as the corporation's average qualifying R&D expenses over the preceding two years—and an enhanced 20% payment on qualifying R&D spending surpassing that two-year average base level. Support under the AB IEG is phased out for corporations with taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, and corporations with taxable capital exceeding $50,000,000 are completely excluded.

body.text: Administrative Governance, Form T661 (Version 26), Pre-Claim Approval (Form T1322), and CRA Audit Procedures
Statutory Filing Deadlines and Electronic Transmission Rules

Under Subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file the prescribed Form T661 alongside T2 Schedule 31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals) within 12 months after the filing-due date of the income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because corporate T2 returns are due 6 months after fiscal year-end, corporations have exactly 18 months from the end of the taxation year to file an SR&ED claim or submit an amended Form T661 to claim forgotten expenditures (for example, for a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end, the absolute statutory deadline was June 30, 2026). Individuals and sole proprietorships have 17.5 months from the end of the tax year to file. If a claimant fails to meet this reporting deadline, the claim is statutorily barred and disallowed. Claimants using approved commercial tax preparation software must submit Form T661 electronically with their return and must not submit duplicate paper copies.
Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Following the Budget 2025 announcements and the enactment of Bill C-15, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. This process enables eligible businesses to obtain a formal determination from the CRA on whether their planned projects meet the statutory definition of SR&ED before starting the work or incurring project costs, with approvals valid for multi-year projects of up to three years.

Per CRA information sheet Cat. Rv4-224/2026E-PD (SR&ED Pre-claim approval), a business qualifies to apply if it operates in Canada, has less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income, is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), a Canadian corporation, or a partnership, and is in good standing with the CRA. The process unfolds across five structured stages. First, the business submits a short web form requesting a pre-claim case number; existing claimants in good standing are contacted within 2 business days through My Business Account, while other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by telephone. Second, the business completes and submits Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval, Parts 1 to 3, Lines 010 to 082) in My Business Account and uploads supporting documents. Each Form T1322 application can cover up to 3 projects, provided the projects represent new work not already claimed and do not involve issues currently under objection or in Tax Court litigation. For each project, Form T1322 requires the project title, anticipated start date, estimated total SR&ED expenditures, field of science or technology, and technical contact person; unlike Part 9 of Form T661, Form T1322 does not ask for external consultant billing arrangements or fees.

Third, all new claimants will be contacted—and existing claimants may be contacted—to schedule a meeting with an SR&ED specialist. Fourth, the CRA issues its formal determination within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application. There is no formal appeal process if pre-claim approval is not granted; however, the business may still undertake the work and submit a regular post-year-end SR&ED claim. Fifth, while pre-claim approval does not replace the mandatory annual filing of Form T661 to substantiate the final quantum of expenditures, claims containing only pre-approved projects that are selected for an expenditure review have their CRA processing times cut in half—from 180 days to 90 days.
Line-by-Line Structure of Form T661 (Version 26 — Updated May 15, 2026)

On May 15, 2026, the CRA released Form T661 (Version 26) alongside interim instructions (which take precedence while Guide T4088 is being rewritten) to reflect Bill C-15. Form T661(26) comprises 10 parts:

In Part 1 — General Information (Lines 010, 050, 100–125), the claimant enters its legal name, tax year, Business Number, total number of projects, financial and technical contacts, and pre-claim approval case numbers. In Part 2 — Project Information (Lines 200–282), the claimant completes one Part 2 per project. If a claimant has more than 20 qualifying projects, it may choose to submit Part 2 for only the 20 largest projects by dollar value at filing, provided it retains completed Part 2 forms for all projects at its place of business and reports every project's cost in Part 6; failure to provide a missing Part 2 upon CRA request results in automatic disallowance of that project's expenditures. Within Part 2, Section A captures project identification, including new Line 207, which requires the first five digits of the research code from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020. Section B houses the three technical narrative fields with strict word limits: Line 242 (maximum 350 words) detailing the scientific or technological uncertainty; Line 244 (maximum 700 words) detailing the systematic work performed (hypotheses, experiments, tests, results, and conclusions in chronological order); and Line 246 (maximum 350 words) detailing the new technical knowledge gained or technological advancement achieved. (For Classified Projects, Section B is omitted from the return and kept on a separate sheet on-site accompanied by an official notification letter to the CRA.) Section C (Lines 270–282) identifies key technical personnel, subcontractors, foreign work indicators, and the mandatory Checklist of Contemporaneous Evidence (Lines 270–282).

In Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures, Section A (Lines 160 and 162) locks in the irrevocable Proxy or Traditional method election. Section B (Lines 300–400) calculates allowable expenditures: Line 300 (directly engaged salaries/wages), Line 315 (unpaid salaries/wages), materials consumed/transformed, arm's length contracts, Line 345 (non-arm's length contracts: deductible, no ITC), restored Line 350 (lease costs after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED), restored Line 355 (Proxy Method only: 50% of lease costs after December 15, 2024, for equipment used 50% to under 90% of the time in SR&ED; Traditional Method enters 0), and Line 360 (Traditional Method overhead and other expenditures). Version 26 splits the total into Line 380 (total current SR&ED expenditures), restored Line 390 (allowable capital expenditures after December 15, 2024), and restored Line 400 (total allowable SR&ED expenditures combining current and capital). Section C computes the Subsection 37(1) deductible pool, adding back assistance repayments (Lines 445, 452, 454) and reporting the current-year deduction on Line 460.

In Part 4 — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 492–570), Version 26 restores the Capital Expenditures column alongside Current Expenditures (reintroducing Lines 496, 504, 514b–514e, 516, 518, 532, 535, 540, 543, 546, and 558), adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 502, strips 20% from arm's length contracts and third-party payments, removes unpaid amounts under Subsection 127(26) on Line 520, and deducts government assistance. Part 5 calculates the salary base (Section A) and the 55% PPA on Line 820 (Section B). Part 6 reports project-by-project costs (including Line 758 for allocated Line 360 overhead). Part 7 and Part 8 capture additional statistical data and the claim checklist. Part 9 — Claim Preparer Information requires complete details on any external preparer and billing arrangements; under Subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, missing, incomplete, or inaccurate information in Part 9 triggers a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable, though the claim itself is not disallowed. Finally, Part 10 contains the authorized signing officer certification.

body.text: CRA Audit Architecture: SARA, Financial Review Reports (FRR), and Cross-Schedule Reconciliations

When evaluating filed claims, the CRA deploys its automated Scientific Research and Experimental Development Risk Assessor (SARA) alongside Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and Financial Reviewers (FRs). For every detailed financial review, the FR must prepare a Financial Review Report (FRR)—previously known as the T20 report—after completing the review plan, working papers, summary of adjustments, and proposal/final letter. The FRR documents the nature and extent of the review, any computer-assisted audit techniques used, and the statutory basis for adjustments, organized into a seven-part summary of adjustments including Section E.1 (adjustments to allowable SR&ED expenditures and the Section 37 pool on Form T661) and Section E.2 (adjustments to qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for ITC).
Per Chapter 3 of the CRA SR&ED Financial Claim Review Manual, Financial Reviewers execute four mandatory cross-schedule reconciliations via the RAPID system:

headers: Key Line Numbers Audited by CRA

cells: T2 Schedule 1 (Net Income (Loss) for Income Tax Purposes)
Line 118 (SR&ED expensed in accounts) Line 231 (Recapture of SR&ED) Lines 290–294 (Other additions) Line 411 (SR&ED deducted in year) Line 499 (Other deductions)

Line 118 adds back accounting R&D expenses; if Line 118 does not match current expenditures on Form T661, the FR demands a formal reconciliation. Line 231 reports negative s. 37(1) pool recapture. Lines 290–294 add back provincial tax credits earned on the notional PPA. Line 411 must equal Line 460 of Form T661. Line 499 deducts ITCs and assistance booked in the income statement.

The FR verifies that all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) SR&ED capital expenditures claimed on Form T661 (Lines 390/400) are not also included as depreciable additions on Schedule 8. Where Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) was claimed in the prior year, the FR verifies that any ITC applied in the prior year related to that SUE is adjusted on Schedule 8.
Parts 1 to 20 (SR&ED Pool, Rate, Refund, Carryback/Carryforward)

The FR verifies the quantum and rate (35% vs. 15%) of ITC claimed, prior-year carryforwards, applications against Part I tax, 3-year carrybacks, and cash refunds. Crucially, the FR confirms that SR&ED capital expenditures claimed on Form T661 are not double-claimed as qualified property in Parts 4 to 7 of Schedule 31.
Individual / Sole Proprietor & Trust ITC Claims

Because limited data from Form T2038(IND) is accessible in RAPID, the FR is instructed to charge out the relevant T1 return or request a copy directly from the individual claimant to verify ITC carryovers and refundability calculations.

body.text: Strategic Audit Defence and Compliance Conclusions

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, alongside Quebec's consolidation of its provincial R&D incentives into the CRIC regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, fundamentally alters the strategic calculus for corporate R&D tax planning in Canada. To maximize non-dilutive capital recovery while insulating claims against CRA technical and financial audit adjustments, Canadian enterprises and their tax advisors must integrate five operational compliance protocols directly into their engineering and accounting workflows.

First, corporate controllers of Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and associated groups must perform dual-basis phase-out modelling prior to filing each annual return. With the enhanced 35% federal expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000 (generating up to $2,100,000 in refundable cash), tax advisors should compare the expanded $15,000,000–$75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out against the newly enacted three-year average gross revenue election. Venture-backed scale-ups carrying substantial preferred equity or convertible debt on their balance sheets should utilize the gross revenue election to prevent balance-sheet capitalisation from eroding their 35% refundable entitlement, while Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) meeting the three-year gross revenue criteria should immediately transition from the 15% non-refundable stream to the 35% refundable stream for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

Second, enterprises investing in GPU compute infrastructure, laboratory instrumentation, or prototyping machinery after December 15, 2024, must implement rigorous operating-time telemetry to substantiate the restored capital and lease expenditure rules. Distinguishing whether an asset satisfies the All or Substantially All (ASA) threshold (claimed on Lines 350 and 390/400 of Form T661(26)), the 50% to under 90% Shared-Use Equipment or proxy lease rule (Line 355), or the Traditional Method incremental lease rule (Line 360) requires contemporaneous usage logs and strict reconciliation with T2 Schedule 8 and Parts 4 to 7 of T2 Schedule 31 to eliminate duplicate CCA or qualified property claims.

Third, eligible businesses with annual gross business income under $25,000,000 embarking on major R&D initiatives should proactively file Form T1322 through My Business Account under the April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process before commencing project work. Securing an upfront three-year eligibility determination within 8 weeks eliminates technical audit risk on up to three proposed projects per application and cuts post-filing expenditure review processing times in half from 180 days to 90 days.

Fourth, in accordance with the Tax Court of Canada's strict evidentiary rulings in Northwest Hydraulic, Hypercube (2015 TCC 65), Zeuter (2006 TCC 597), and Concept Danat (2019 TCC 32), technical narratives in Part 2, Section B of Form T661(26) (Lines 242, 244, and 246) must eliminate business hyperbole and "trial and error" phrasing. Engineering teams must embed SR&ED tracking into their operating system—recording technological uncertainties as they arise, documenting the analytical reason why each failed experimental iteration failed before testing the next hypothesis, and preserving immutable repository commit hashes, timestamps, and failed test data. Finally, prior to electronic transmission within the 18-month corporate statutory deadline, tax preparers must ensure that the five-digit Statistics Canada CRDC 2020 code is entered on Line 207, that Part 9 claim preparer disclosures are complete to avoid the $1,000 joint and several penalty, and that T2 Schedule 1 (Lines 118, 231, 290–294, 411, and 499), T2 Schedule 8, T2 Schedule 31, and provincial schedules (Ontario Schedules 508 and 566, Quebec CRIC and CDAEIA filings, or Alberta AT1 IEG claims) reconcile to the dollar against the financial statements.
